newsitem.title: INDIA: India denies missile deployment on Pakistan border.
newsitem.headline: India denies missile deployment on Pakistan border.

text.p: India on Wednesday denied a U.S. newspaper report that it had deployed medium-range ballistic missiles along its border with arch-rival Pakistan.
"Prithvi missiles have not been deployed along the international border," a Defence Ministry spokesman told Reuters.
The Defence Ministry on Tuesday said it had no information on the Washington Post report, which appeared in Tuesday's editions.
Pakistan had voiced serious concern over the alleged deployment and said the move could trigger "a dangerous ballistic arms race" in South Asia.
Earlier on Wednesday, Pakistan's army chief said Islamabad must develop an "indigenous capability" to meet a perceived missile threat from India.
The United States on Tuesday declared itself in "outright opposition" to the deployment of ballistic missiles by India and Pakistan, and said it was working to prevent such a move.

But U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns, speaking at a news briefing in Washington, said the United States had still not decided that India had moved such weapons to a prospective launch site.

The Washington Post report said U.S. intelligence agencies had concluded that less than a dozen of the surface-to-surface Prithvi missiles were now located near the city of Jullundur in Punjab state in northwest India.

India has successfully tested the 250-km (150-mile) Prithvi missile and a 150-km (90-mile) variation, and has vowed to press ahead with its missile programme despite opposition from the United States and other countries.

India says its missile programme is in response to the "evolving security environment" in South Asia -- a reference to weapons programmes being pursued by neighbouring China, with which it went to war in 1962, and Pakistan, with which it has fought three wars since 1947.

India's 2,500-km (1,500-mile) Agni missile is regarded as a potential deterrent to China while the Prithvi is considered more suited as a deterrent against Pakistan. Both missiles are considered capable of carrying nuclear warheads.

India and Pakistan say they have no nuclear arms but experts say either can assemble them swiftly. India held its only nuclear test in 1974. Pakistan says it has achieved nuclear capability without conducting a single test.

Both Pakistan and nuclear-armed China deny Western reports that Beijing transferred to Islamabad nuclear weapons components and Chinese M-11 missiles that can deliver nuclear warheads. But India views their close ties with considerable concern.
